items.title: Show HN: Director's Lookbook, named looks for image, video and music prompts
items.description:
Show HN: River Road Labs is a small artisanal studio based out of Central NJ. We built this tool to scratch our own itch. As AI video and image capabilities get more sophisticated we found that we struggled at times to find the words to describe the aesthetic style we were shooting (no pun) for. Other times it is good to just have a massive resource of styles and imagery to flip through at random and to let serendipity do the rest. Director's Lookbook lets you type a feeling and get dealt a set of style cards with prompt text to use. No more copying or saving prompts, use the tool. The feeling reader is a small hosted model with a free daily allowance. The MCP server is read only, no auth, no key, it works in Claude as a connector and in Cursor as well. Setup is at directorslookbook.app/mcp. The connector keeps no request text, only daily counts of which tools were called. The tool is free, no login, no account. We welcome feedback on how to make the tool better and what looks are missing! Thanks!
Website metadata: Director's Lookbook: 798 named looks: an AI style library for image, video and music prompts. Cinematic prompts, camera angles, film looks, colour grades and music styles, no artist names. Say the feeling, get the look, copy the prompt.

items.title: Show HN: Open-source multi-player artifacts that update themselves
items.description:
Show HN: Rally is a multi-player platform to build reactive micro-applications together that connects event streams to agents that then update the artifact. We've had pilots build a PR dashboard that sorts by risk assessment (an agent actually reads the code) per PR, a micro-CRM that pulls in live deals from multiple Gmail inboxes, and a shared grocery list that groups items by store aisle. We're similar to Muse's Spaces, Google's TableTop, and the standard artifacts most harnesses now support. Our differentiator is being multi-player so groups can iterate together, artifacts calling agents on incoming events so updates can be more sophisticated than an API call, and giving artifacts a full application stack. Under the hood, each artifact is a Cloudflare Durable Object with its own SQLite database, compute, and storage. As an example this is our podcast artifact that helps us keep up-to-date on what happened on the repo each day https://connected-tidy-crystalline-haldane-g.rallyuserconten... GitHub: https://github.com/juno-ai-labs/avalon
Website metadata: Rally creates reactive, multi-human artifacts: dashboards, micro-apps, podcast feeds, websites and team tools that react to events in the services you already use, and that your team shapes together.

items.title: Show HN: TrnRT – An open-source LLM inference engine for AWS Trainium
items.description:
Show HN: Hi HN, Sanchit here from RunAnywhere (YC W26). We just open-sourced TrnRT: Trainium RunTime, our inference engine for AWS Trainium. We started 3 weeks back, and currently we’re able to serve and run GLM 5.3 flash (FP8) on AWS trn2.48xlarge, and will bring more models support soon. It’s open to contributions :) What it does today: - Serves 2 instances of GLM-5.3 flash on a single box, 8 trn2 with a cache aware router. - Can process 3.57M TPM (tokens per minute) on SemiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks. - Runs decode as one NKI kernel per layer half, or for the 11 sparse-attention layers fuses both blocks into a single kernel, for faster performance. We started working on Trn2 because we wanted to explore it and see if we can come close to beating it’s performance in terms of cost efficiency compared to H100/H200. A big MoE with 1M context window such as GLM-5.3 flash requires a lot of memory, and memory/tb on a trn2.48xlarge costs less than half compared to 8x h200 on AWS, and hence we wanted to experiment with it and now we’re sharing some early results. But AWS's own stack didn't support the model: vLLM Neuron's latest release did not register any GLM model, and NxDI, AWS's own distributed inference framework, is no longer under active development. We also saw the drop of SGLang Neuron implementation yesterday, but there is no good support for Trn2, which is the only chip available for public use right now. We ran semiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks, which replays real coding agent sessions: - 1 box served 28.9 RPM(requests per minute) with 32 agents at batch 12 (also known as concurrency) -The P50 TTFT with a cached prompt at 16 agents is ~1.24 seconds with a decode of 35.9 tps. Initially, the recurrence in one kda (linear attention) layer was ~2% of the layer's attention time at batch 1, and the rest was projections, transposes and XLA glue between small kernels. So we wrote the megakernel so that it covers the whole layer in 2 kernel dispatch, which made decode 25% faster at batch 8. The sparse attention kernel keep a layer’s working weights in SBUF, distributing weighted streaming across the cores and handling the interchip communication within There’s an approximation in the sparse-attention prefill, affecting about 1.2% of block selections. You can refer to the write-up for the profiling results: https://runanywhere.ai/blog/glm-5-3-flash-trainium2-nki-mega... Please give it a try yourself on a trn2.48xlarge and reproduce the AgentX results by following the

items.title: Show HN: Belay – formal verification for SQLite migrations and queries in Lean 4
items.description:
Show HN: Hi, I'm Tzanko and I'm the author of Belay. Belay is a Lean 4 library for doing formal verification of SQLite queries and migrations. It implements a semantic model of a subset of SQLite, validated by differential tests that compare the output against native SQLite. With Belay I wanted to see how difficult it is to use formal verification for everyday development tasks. It turns out it can be made not much harder than writing an integration test: you state the claim, the agent writes the proof, and Lean's kernel checks it, so the only thing you have to read is the claim (longer write-up on the motivation and agent workflow: https://vihren.dev/blog/20261112-belay/ ). While a migration is being written, your agent can run #sql_check, which searches small databases for counterexamples to a claim, and is as easy to run as a linter. Once the migration is settled, the agent writes a proof of the claims you need, for example that the migration preserves the results of existing queries and succeeds on valid data. Currently Belay supports a subset of SQLite 3.51.0, cross-checked against native SQLite on 5,768 differential test cases, most of which come from SQLite's own test suite. Unsupported SQL is rejected with a reason and never approximated. Not every rule of the model has had a human audit yet. The model covers single-connection operational semantics only: it says nothing about query plans, locks, concurrency or crash behavior. I think this approach can make formal verification as routine as testing, though two things stand in the way. The first is coverage: the model has to cover the full semantics of SQLite and all of its recent versions, and the same work has to be done for other engines such as PostgreSQL and ClickHouse. The second is proof cost: the proofs of common claims are still long for the agent to write, and they have to become short. I'm looking for design partners who want this for their workloads on SQLite or other open-source databases, because a real workload is the best guide to what to cover first. The models that come out of that work become part of Belay as open source. Reach out at [email removed]. If you know a tricky SQLite edge case where the model might diverge from native SQLite, or a gnarly migration bug you've hit in production, I'd love to test it and hear your thoughts.
Website metadata: Lean-based verification of SQLite schema migrations - vihren-dev/belay
items.product_description: Lean-based verification of SQLite schema migrations - vihren-dev/belay

items.title: Show HN: Open-source, real-time object tracking for live video feeds
items.description:
Show HN: I type "forklift" on a live warehouse camera, and tamserve finds and tracks both forklifts, including the one driving in. Then I add "person" without stopping it. tamserve runs Meta's SAM 3 on live camera feeds. SAM 3's own tracker handles one recorded video at a time, runs at about 8 fps, and runs out of memory on long videos. tamserve uses SAM 3 to find objects every few frames and a lightweight tracker (EdgeTAM) to follow them in between, with one copy of each model shared across all your cameras. *On one RTX 4090:* * *Any object you name:* 4x faster than SAM 3's tracker, at 92% of its accuracy * *People:* 16 cameras at once, 14x less GPU per frame, and slightly more accurate than SAM 3 (89.6 vs 87.8 HOTA) * *Memory:* flat at 3.5 GB on a 3,000 frame video, where SAM 3 runs out at frame 423 *Worth a look if you're building:* * Warehouse or factory safety (forklifts, pallets, hard hats) * Security or retail camera analytics * Home or elder care monitoring * Robotics, wildlife or lab monitoring * Annotation tools for long videos `pip install "tamserve[sam3]"` Please give me any and all feedback or edit tamserve to meet your needs, and a star helps if you find it useful!
Website metadata: Live, multi-camera object tracking with SAM3, SAM 2 and EdgeTAM, on one GPU or many. One model per GPU serves every camera: faster than the original code, about 4x less GPU memory, identical masks. - aryamandarda/tamserve
items.product_description: Live, multi-camera object tracking with SAM3, SAM 2 and EdgeTAM, on one GPU or many. One model per GPU serves every camera: faster than the original code, about 4x less GPU memory, identical masks. - aryamandarda/tamserve
